title: The rhinoceros horn
hookLine: a poem whose every verse ends: wander alone like the rhinoceros horn
last: MY HUT IS OPEN, MY FIRE IS OUT.

cards: The Indian rhinoceros has one horn. One. And it mostly keeps to itself, grazing through tall grass by the rivers, a huge animal that doesn't travel in a herd.
In the British Library there's a birch-bark scroll, written in a language called Gandhari, which its editor dates to around the first century.
It's among the oldest Buddhist manuscripts known, and one of the texts on it is a poem about that animal.

teach.b: The poem is the third in the Sutta Nipata, the Khaggavisana Sutta, a long run of verses. Verse after verse ends with the same Pali refrain: eko care khaggavisanakappo. Wander alone, like the rhinoceros horn.

Visana is a horn, and khaggavisana names the rhinoceros horn: one horn on the animal's head, one walker in the world. Some translators say like the rhinoceros, some say like its horn; the image works either way.
The verses ask you to set things down. Violence toward every living being: wish harm to none. Not wishing even for a son, let alone a companion.
Closeness breeds attachment, they say, and attachment breeds sorrow. Be like a deer in the forest, unbound, going wherever it wants to graze.

teach.h: A DEER, A LION, THE WIND, A LOTUS
teach.b: Like a lion not startled by sounds, the wind not caught in a net, a lotus not stained by water.
Is this lonely? The poem doesn't sound lonely. It sounds free.

The old commentary says these verses were spoken by solitary buddhas, people who woke up on their own and lived without a community. That's the tradition's reading; the poem itself just keeps returning to the one horn.
And it isn't the whole story: early on, a few verses turn a corner, and those are tomorrow's.
For today, stay with the rhinoceros: steady, unhurried, needing no one's permission to walk through the grass.

how: Buddhist monastics and lay practitioners sometimes take periods of solitary retreat, and Theravada teachers draw on the rhinoceros poem's refrain, eko care khaggavisanakappo, when they speak about solitude.

games.q: you're the wanderer in the poem. old friends want you back in the crowd, every night, every party. what does the refrain say?
o: go along so no one is hurt.
wander alone, like the rhinoceros horn.
argue until they agree with you.
games.why: verse after verse comes back to the same line: wander alone. tomorrow, the poem adds an important exception.

practice: Feel your own weight settle onto the ground, the way the rhinoceros feels the earth under it, and breathe steadily, with nobody watching and nobody needing to approve.
Let each breath go the way the poem walks: not running from anyone, not looking for anyone.

wordCard.voice: khaggavisana. The refrain of the Sutta Nipata's third poem: wander alone, like the one horn of the Indian rhinoceros, steady and free. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali khaggavisana: rhinoceros horn, the name of Sn 1.3.

carryVoice: Your line: alone like the rhinoceros. Steady and free, not lonely. That's day five hundred seventy-nine.
